nodes.title: Theory — Sampling distributions / CLT
nodes.content:
## G11 — Sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

When we draw a sample of size $n$ from a population and compute a statistic (e.g. sample mean $\bar X$, sample proportion $\bar P$), the statistic itself has a **distribution** — the *sampling distribution*.

### Sample mean distribution
For independent $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ from a population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$:
$$
\bar X = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i, \qquad E[\bar X] = \mu, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2/n.
$$

If the population is normal: $\bar X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$ exactly.

**Central Limit Theorem (CLT):** for $n$ large (rule of thumb $n \ge 30$, or $n \ge 40$ if heavy-tailed), $\bar X$ is *approximately* normal **regardless of the population distribution**.

### Sample proportion distribution
For $X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$, the sample proportion $\bar P = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i$ has
$$
E[\bar P] = p, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\bar P) = \frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$
For $n$ large (typically $np \ge 10$ and $n(1-p) \ge 10$), by CLT:
$$
\bar P \approx N\!\left(p,\; \frac{p(1-p)}{n}\right).
$$

### Probability calculations
Same R commands as for any normal — just plug in the **sampling-distribution parameters**:

%%RBLOCK%%
`pnorm(value, mean=mu_population, sd=sigma_population/sqrt(n))    # P(X-bar <= value)`
`pnorm(value, mean=p,             sd=sqrt(p*(1-p)/n))             # P(P-bar <= value)`
%%/RBLOCK%%


### When can we apply CLT vs need normality?
- Large sample → CLT applies → no need to assume population normal.
- Small sample → must assume population is normal to use the same formulas.

nodes.title: Ex 4.3d — Probability that 150 customers spend > 1980 total
nodes.content:
**Question.** Consider the 150 customers in a store: what is the probability that at least 80% will spend more than 12 Euros to purchase private label products?

---

**Answer.** Define $p$ = probability one customer spends > 12 Euros = 0.8413. With $n = 150$ customers, the proportion of customers $\bar P$ exceeding the threshold follows approximately

$$
\bar P \sim N\left(0.8413,\; \frac{0.8413(1-0.8413)}{150}\right).
$$

The probability that the proportion is at least 80%:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(0.8, 0.8413, sqrt(0.8413*(1-0.8413)/150))`
`## ≈ 0.9075`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 4.4 a1 — Probability of delivery time exceeding 90 min
nodes.content:
**Question.** Considering the delivery time exceeding 90 minutes — the journey time $X$ is normally distributed with mean 80 and SD 25 — what is the probability that the random variable $Y = X - 90$ is positive?

---

**Answer.** $Y$ follows a normal distribution and the standard normal distribution; therefore $(80 - 90)/\sigma$ is the first quartile of a standard normal distribution.


%%RBLOCK%%
`pnorm(0, -10, 25)`
`## [1] 0.6554217`
%%/RBLOCK%%


So $(80 - 90)/25 = -0.6745$, leading to $-0.6748$. Therefore $X \sim N(90, 14.826^2)$.

**a2)** The probability that a generic workday without any special events, the bus takes more than 2 hours to travel the entire route, $\Pr(X > 120)$:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(120, mean=90, sd=14.826)`
`## [1] 0.0211524`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 4.4b — P(travel time > 82 min) and 30th percentile
nodes.content:
**Question.** The bus that travels exceeded 70% of the days. What is the 30-th percentile?

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`qnorm(0.3, 90, 14.826)`
`## [1] 82.2524`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The variable indicating whether the bus takes less than 82 minutes to complete its entire route has a Bernoulli distribution with parameter $p$ = probability that the bus takes less than 82 minutes:

%%RBLOCK%%
`pnorm(82, 90, 14.826)`
`## [1] 0.294739`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The proportion of buses over 45 taking less than 82 minutes, $\bar P_n$, has a distribution that can be approximated by the Central Limit Theorem:

$$
\bar P \approx N(p, p(1-p)/n) \;=\; N(0.2954, 0.0207)
$$

The probability that the bus takes in total less than 82 minutes on at least 10% of the days:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(0.10, 0.295, sqrt((0.295*(1-0.295))/45))`
`## [1] 0.9979317`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 4.9a — P(sample mean Sales < 22500) — pizzeria sampling
nodes.content:
**Question.** A sample of size 81 pizzerias in the winter season. Sales of single pizzerias have mean 25000 and SD 9800/$\sqrt{81}$. Probability that the sample mean is less than 22500?

---

**Answer.** Since the sample is large enough, by the Central Limit Theorem no assumptions on the distribution of the turnover in the population are needed and the distribution of the mean of a sample of size 81 can be approximated by a Normal distribution, $\bar X \sim N(25000, 9800^2/81)$.


%%RBLOCK%%
`pnorm(22500, 25000, sqrt(9800^2/81))`
`## [1] 0.0104027`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 4.9b — P(sample mean > 24800) — pizzeria sampling
nodes.content:
**Question.** Probability that the mean turnover on the drawn sample is greater than 24800?

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(24800, 25000, sqrt(9800^2/81))`
`## [1] 0.5728855`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 4.9c — P(mean is between 23000 and 27000)
nodes.content:
**Question.** To determine the probability that the mean turnover of the pizzerias in the sample is between 23000 and 27000, in a sample of size 20.

---

**Answer.** It is necessary to assume that the turnover in the population of all pizzerias is normally distributed. Under this assumption, the distribution of the mean of a sample of size 20 is $\bar X \sim N(25000, 9800^2/20)$, and $\Pr(23000 < \bar X < 27000)$ is:


%%RBLOCK%%
`pnorm(27000, 25000, sqrt(9800^2/20)) - pnorm(23000, 25000, sqrt(9800^2/20))`
`## [1] 0.6385896`
%%/RBLOCK%%


Without performing further calculations, we expect this probability to be lower if the sample is of size 10 instead of 20, since the distribution of the sample mean would be more dispersed around the mean (as a consequence of a larger standard error).

**d1)** The mean of turnover in samples of size 100 has a distribution that, by the central limit theorem, can be approximated by $\bar X \sim N(25000, 9800^2/100)$. The mean turnover in the sample considered in the dataframe `pizzerie` is $\bar x_n = 23947$:


%%RBLOCK%%
`distr.summary.x(Sales, stats=c("mean","sd"), data=pizzerie)`
`##  n n.a  mean   sd`
`## 100 0  23946.99  9538.62`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The probability that the mean of turnover in samples of size 100 is greater than the final found in this specific sample, $\Pr(\bar X > 23947)$, is:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(23947, 25000, 980)`
`## [1] 0.8586984`
%%/RBLOCK%%


**d2)** To define the extreme mean turnover we need to find the 1-st and 99-th percentile of the distribution of the mean of samples of size 100:

%%RBLOCK%%
`qnorm(0.01, 25000, sqrt(9800^2/100))`
`## [1] 22720.18`
`qnorm(0.99, 25000, sqrt(9800^2/100))`
`## [1] 27279.82`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The samples with 1% extreme mean turnover are those with a mean smaller than 22720 and higher than 27280 Euro.

nodes.title: Ex 4.10 a1 — Pr(extreme 5% sample mean of AmountSpent)
nodes.content:
**Question.** Since the sample is large enough, by the Central Limit Theorem no assumptions on the distribution of the amount spent in the population is needed and the distribution of the mean of a sample of size 750 can be approximated by a Normal distribution.

---

**Answer.** $\bar X \sim N(1000, 810000/750)$.

**a2)** The mean volume reached by the 5% of the largest sample means is the 95-th percentile, $p95$, of the distribution of the sample mean:

%%RBLOCK%%
`qnorm(0.95, mean=1000, sd=sqrt(810000/750))`
`## [1] 1054.055`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The range of values including the 95% of the "central" values of the distribution of the sample mean is the interval between the values $x_{0.025}$ and $x_{0.975}$ such that $\Pr(\bar X > x_{0.975}) = 0.975$ and $\Pr(\bar X < x_{0.025}) = 0.025$:

%%RBLOCK%%
`qnorm(0.025, mean=1000, sd=sqrt(810000/750))`
`## [1] 935.589`
`qnorm(0.975, mean=1000, sd=sqrt(810000/750))`
`## [1] 1064.411`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The mean amount in the sample considered in the dataframe DS is 1228.44 and does not belong to that range.

%%RBLOCK%%
`mean(DS$AmountSpent)`
`## [1] 1228.437`
%%/RBLOCK%%


Thus, the **available sample** has an extremely high mean, being higher than the value exceeded by the 2.5% of all the means of samples size 750.

**a3)** The percentage of samples of size 750 with a mean of the amount spent greater than 1228.4 is $100\bar P_n(1228.4)$ and is approximately 0:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(1228.437, mean=1000, sd=sqrt(810000/750))`
`## [1] 1.831995e-12`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 4.10b — Sample proportion (CLT for proportions)
nodes.content:
**Question.** The proportion observed in the sample is in the dataframe DS is 0.704.

---

**Answer.**


%%RBLOCK%%
`distr.table.x(Location, freq="prop", data=DS)`
`##  Close Far`
`##  0.704 0.296`
%%/RBLOCK%%


Therefore, the probability that the sample proportion of (a generic) sample of size 750 is higher than the observed, $\Pr(\bar P > 0.704)$, is:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(0.704, mean=0.69, sd=sqrt((0.69*(1-0.69))/750))`
`## [1] 0.2035329`
%%/RBLOCK%%


**b2)** The interval that includes the 50% of the less extreme values for the sample proportion if we consider samples of size 750 is the interval between the first and third quartile of the distribution:

%%RBLOCK%%
`qnorm(0.25, mean=0.69, sd=sqrt((0.69*(1-0.69))/750))`
`## [1] 0.6786093`
`qnorm(0.75, mean=0.69, sd=sqrt((0.69*(1-0.69))/750))`
`## [1] 0.7013907`
%%/RBLOCK%%


**b3)** The probability of extracting samples of size 1000 characterized by a sample proportion greater than 0.72, $\Pr(\bar P > 0.72)$:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(0.72, mean=0.69, sd=sqrt((0.69*(1-0.69))/1000))`
`## [1] 0.01978318`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The probability would be lower if the same population would be observed in the smaller sample of size 1000 because the distribution of the sample proportion would be more concentrated around the center due to a lower standard error.

nodes.title: Ex 4.12a — Pr(customer spends > 80 Euro at first purchase)
nodes.content:
**Question.** Let $X$ be the r.v. describing the amount spent at first purchase; we assume that $X \sim N(60, 25^2)$. The probability that a generic clients spends more than 80 Euro is $\Pr(X > 80)$.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(80, 60, 25)`
`## [1] 0.2118554`
%%/RBLOCK%%


**b)** Let $\bar P$ describe the random variable describing the proportion of clients who spend more than 80 Euro at their first purchase among a sample of 150 new clients. Since the number of new clients is high enough the distribution of the sample proportion can be approximated by a normal distribution:

$$
\bar P \approx N(0.212, 0.212(1-0.212)/150).
$$

And the probability that the proportion is 20% maximum is $\Pr(\bar P \le 0.2)$:

%%RBLOCK%%
`pnorm(0.2, mean=0.212, sd=sqrt(0.212*(1-0.212)/150))`
`## [1] 0.3611689`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 4.12b — Pr(sample sum > 9100)
nodes.content:
**Question.** Let's indicate the turnover from the campaign that is by the total amount spent by 150 new clients at their first purchase. Is it possible that $\Pr(S > 9100) = 0$?

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(9100, 150*60, 150*sqrt(25^2))`
`## [1] 0.3719857`
%%/RBLOCK%%


or

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(9100, 9000, sqrt(93750))`
`## [1] 0.3719857`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The same result could be obtained also considering that the r.v. $Y = S - 9100$ is given as the total amount spent by 150 new clients at their first purchase) is distributed as $Y \sim N(150\cdot 60 - 9100, 150\cdot 25^2) = N(-100, 93750)$. Therefore, the probability that the total amount spent is higher than the cost is $\Pr(Y > 0) = 0.372$, obtained as:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(0, -100, sqrt(93750))`
`## [1] 0.3719857`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 4.13 — Linear normal + CLT for proportion
nodes.content:
**Question.** Let $X$ be amount spent by a customer; $E[X] = 12, Var(X) = 5^2$. The total amount spent by a sample of $n = 80$ customers is the random variable $S = X_1 + \ldots + X_{80}$ ($X_i$ iid).

---

**Answer.** Assumptions: each customer's amount is independent. Since the sample is large enough, by the central limit theorem the distribution of $S$ is approximately normal: $S \sim N(80\cdot 12, 80\cdot 25) = N(960, 2000)$. The required probability is $\Pr(S > 1000) = 0.1855$:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(1000, mean=960, sd=sqrt(2000))`
`## [1] 0.1855467`
%%/RBLOCK%%


**b)** Let $\bar P$ be the r.v. describing the proportion of customers spending more than 1000 Euro in the 115 shops, then we have that approximately:

$$
\bar P \approx N\left(0.1855,\; \frac{0.1855(1-0.1855)}{115}\right).
$$

The probability of the sample proportion being less than 0.15 is therefore $\Pr(\bar P < 0.15) = 0.166$:

%%RBLOCK%%
`pnorm(0.15, 0.1855, sqrt(0.1855*(1-0.1855)/115))`
`## [1] 0.163397`
%%/RBLOCK%%


Or with rounding:

%%RBLOCK%%
`pnorm(0.15, 0.1855, sqrt(0.1855*(1-0.1855)/115))`
`## [1] 0.1636914`
`# or rounding to 3 decimals`
`pnorm(0.15, 0.185, sqrt(0.185*(1-0.185)/115))`
`## [1] 0.166869`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: P1-2024 Ex6a — CLT: P(total spend > 1000) for n=80 customers
nodes.content: A shop expects more than 1000 euros in the next hour. Specify clearly whether and what assumptions are needed to determine the required probability. Let $X$ = amount spent by a customer; we know $E[X] = 12$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 5^2 = 25$. The total amount spent by a sample of $n = 80$ customers is the random variable $S = X_1 + \cdots + X_{80}$. Compute $P(S > 1000)$. --- **Answer.** **Assumptions:** the $X_i$ are i.i.d. (independent customers, same spend distribution). Since $n = 80$ is large, by the CLT the sum is approximately normal regardless of the distribution of an individual customer. Thus $S \;\dot\sim\; N(n\mu,\, n\sigma^2) = N(80 \cdot 12,\, 80 \cdot 25) = N(960,\, 2000)$. Standardising: $z = (1000-960)/\sqrt{2000} = 40/44.72 \approx 0.894$, so $P(S > 1000) = 1 - \Phi(0.894) \approx 0.1855$. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `p_S <- 1 - pnorm(1000, mean=960, sd=sqrt(2000))` `p_S` `## [1] 0.1855467` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: P1-2024 Ex6b — Sample proportion of shops
nodes.content: Assume that in the city there are $115$ shops with the same characteristics as those considered in point a, and assume that exactly $80$ customers in each outlet take advantage of the promotion. What is the probability that the proportion of outlets where the $80$ customers spend more than $1000$ euros in total is less than $0.15$? (If you did not answer point a, assume the required probability was $0.2$). Let $\hat P$ be the random variable describing the proportion of customers spending more than $1000$ euros in the $115$ shops. From point a we have $\pi \approx 0.1855$, so $\hat P$ is approximately $$\hat P \sim N\!\left(0.1855,\; \frac{0.1855 \cdot (1-0.1855)}{115}\right)$$ --- **Answer.** By the CLT, the sampling distribution of $\hat P$ is approximately Normal with mean $\pi \approx 0.1855$ and variance $\pi(1-\pi)/n = 0.1855 \cdot 0.8145 / 115$. The required probability is therefore $$P(\hat P < 0.15) \approx 0.166$$ **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `pnorm(0.15, 0.1855, sqrt(0.1855*0.8145/115))` `## [1] 0.1636914` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: P1-2025 Ex2a — SE of sample proportion (Shares=low vs high)
nodes.content: For Shares=high ($\hat p = 0.32$, $n = 550$) and Shares=low ($\hat p = 0.173$, $n = 550$), compute the standard errors. --- **Answer.** $SE(\hat p_{\text{high}}) = \sqrt{0.32(1-0.32)/550} = 0.020$. $SE(\hat p_{\text{low}}) = \sqrt{0.173(1-0.173)/550} = 0.016$. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `sqrt(0.32*(1-0.32)/550)` `sqrt(0.173*(1-0.173)/550)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: P1-2025 Ex2b — Misinterpretation of SE
nodes.content: Can we conclude from a lower SE that the *specific* estimate is closer to the parameter? Justify. --- **Answer.** **No.** A lower SE means generic estimates from this estimator are more tightly clustered around the unknown parameter on average. It does NOT measure the distance of any *specific* realised estimate from the parameter. No conclusion can be drawn about accuracy of a single observed estimate. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# Simulate to see SE is a property of the estimator, not a single estimate` `set.seed(1); sims <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(50, mean=0, sd=1)))` `sd(sims) # empirical SE of x-bar` `## [1] 0.1410` `1/sqrt(50) # theoretical SE` `## [1] 0.1414` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: P1-2026 Ex6a — Sample means and SE for Aggregator/Airline
nodes.content: From the channel summary table compute $\bar x$ and $SE(\bar x)$ for Aggregator and Airline. --- **Answer.** Aggregator: $\bar x = 56.22$, $s = 12.13$, $n = 142$ → $SE = 12.13/\sqrt{142} = 1.0179$. Airline: $\bar x = 53.50$, $s = 22.06$, $n = 224$ → $SE = 22.06/\sqrt{224} = 1.4739$. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `distr.summary.x(x=PaidFare, by=Channel, data=Bidding)` `12.13/sqrt(142) # Aggregator SE` `22.06/sqrt(224) # Airline SE` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: P1-2026 Ex6b — Reliability of PaidFare estimate vs SE: cannot conclude
nodes.content: Can we conclude one specific PaidFare estimate is more reliable from a smaller SE? --- **Answer.** **No conclusions can be drawn.** Although $SE(\bar x_{Aggregator}) < SE(\bar x_{Airline})$, SE refers to the sampling distribution of the *estimator* — the deviation of a *generic* estimate from the parameter — NOT to the deviation of a *specific* realised PaidFare estimate. We can say the Aggregator estimator is more reliable (its estimates are *on average* more tightly clustered around the population mean), but we cannot draw conclusions about the reliability of specific realised PaidFare estimates or their distance from the corresponding parameter. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# SE compares estimators (long-run), not single PaidFare estimates` `SE_agg <- 12.13/sqrt(142) # 1.018` `SE_air <- 22.06/sqrt(224) # 1.474` `# A single Airline PaidFare x-bar could still land closer to mu than a single Aggregator one` `c(SE_agg, SE_air)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Theory — Linear combinations
nodes.content:
## G12 — Linear combinations of independent random variables

Given $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ independent random variables (not necessarily normal) and constants $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n$, define
$$
Y = a_0 + \sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i.
$$

### Expectation (always linear)
$$
E[Y] = a_0 + \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\, E[X_i].
$$
This holds **regardless** of dependence between the $X_i$.

### Variance (requires independence or covariance terms)
$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X_i) + 2\sum_{i<j} a_i a_j \mathrm{Cov}(X_i, X_j).
$$
If the $X_i$ are independent (so all covariances are zero), the cross terms vanish.

### If the $X_i$ are normal
Any linear combination of independent normals is again normal:
$$
Y \sim N\!\left(a_0 + \sum_i a_i \mu_i,\; \sum_i a_i^2 \sigma_i^2\right).
$$
This is the key result behind weighted-average grades, total spending across customers, etc.

### Common applications
- **Sum** $S = X_1 + \ldots + X_n$ of $n$ iid normals $X_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$: $S \sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)$.
- **Weighted average** of grades: e.g. $G = 0.4 X + 0.6 Y$ → $E[G] = 0.4 \mu_X + 0.6 \mu_Y$, etc.
- **Difference** $D = X - Y$: $E[D] = \mu_X - \mu_Y$, $\mathrm{Var}(D) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y) - 2\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)$.

### Bivariate normal
$(X, Y)$ jointly normal with means $\mu_X, \mu_Y$, variances $\sigma_X^2, \sigma_Y^2$ and correlation $\rho$:
- Marginals: $X \sim N(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2)$, $Y \sim N(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y^2)$.
- Linear combination $aX + bY \sim N(a\mu_X + b\mu_Y, a^2\sigma_X^2 + b^2\sigma_Y^2 + 2ab\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y)$.

nodes.title: Ex 4.5 — Total time = sum of two normal sequential events
nodes.content:
**Question.** Two sequential events $D$ and $B$. The total time $D + B$ required to pass both checks: compute $E[Y]$ and $Var(Y)$.

---

**Answer.** Given $X = D + B$ and assuming independence, $E[Y] = E[D] + E[B] = 13$ and $Var(Y) = Var(D) + Var(B) + 2\mathrm{Cov}(D, B) = 2\rho_{D,B}\sigma_D\sigma_B + 1 + 2 = 4.3735 - 6.75$.

Therefore $Y \sim N(13, 6.75)$.

**b)** We need to compute the 90-th percentile of the distribution of the total time required to pass both checks, which corresponds to the 10% longest times it could take:

%%RBLOCK%%
`qnorm(0.9, 13, sqrt(6.75))`
`## [1] 16.32957`
%%/RBLOCK%%

If the flight leaves at 5 pm you should therefore arrive at around 3.59 pm.

nodes.title: Ex 4.6 — Sum/difference of normals: E and Var
nodes.content:
**Question.** Combine two normals via a linear combination.

---

**Answer.** Let $D = X + B$ where $X \sim N(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2)$ and $B \sim N(\mu_B, \sigma_B^2)$. Then $D$ is normally distributed with mean $E[D] = E[X] + E[B]$ and variance $Var(D) = Var(X) + Var(B)$ (assuming independence).

To compute the probability that the sum exceeds a threshold:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(threshold, mean=E_D, sd=sqrt(Var_D))`
%%/RBLOCK%%


Equivalent works for the difference $D - B$ — mean subtracts, variance adds.

nodes.title: Ex 4.7 — Probability both checks pass — joint distribution
nodes.content:
**Question.** What is the probability that both checks $X$ and $D$ pass — i.e. the joint distribution of $X = D + B$ requires both events?

---

**Answer.** $E(Y) = E[B] + E[D] = 13$ and $Var(Y) = Var(B) + Var(D) + 2\mathrm{Cov}(B, D) = 1.6 + 1 + 2\cdot 1.4375 = 6.75$.

Therefore $Y \sim N(13, 6.75)$.

**b)** We need to compute the 90-th percentile of the distribution of the total time required to pass both checks, which corresponds to the 10% longest times it could take.

%%RBLOCK%%
`qnorm(0.9, 13, sqrt(6.75))`
`## [1] 16.32957`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 4.8a — Bivariate normal G = 0.4X + 0.6Y: E[G] and Var[G]
nodes.content:
**Question.** Let $G$ denote the final grade, $G = 0.4X + 0.6Y$. Compute $E[G]$ and $Var[G]$ given $X \sim N(25, 4²)$ and $Y \sim N(28, 4²)$ with $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = 0$ and $(X, Y)$ jointly Bernoulli/normal.

---

**Answer.**

$$
E[G] = 0.4\cdot E[X] + 0.6\cdot E[Y] = 0.4\cdot 25 + 0.6\cdot 28 = 26.8.
$$

$$
Var[G] = 0.4^2 Var[X] + 0.6^2 Var[Y] + 2\cdot 0.4\cdot 0.6\cdot \mathrm{Cov}(X, Y).
$$

Computing $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = \rho_{X,Y}\sigma_X\sigma_Y$:

%%RBLOCK%%
`0.25 * (5.04 * sqrt(24.616))`
`## [1] 4.0953`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The internal consistency between the 50% central votes can be determined only under the assumption that the joint distribution of $(X, Y)$ is a bivariate normal. In this case, $G \sim N(26.8, 24.616)$ and the range of the 50% central votes is the interval between the first and third quartile, which has amplitude:

%%RBLOCK%%
`qnorm(0.25, 25.04, sqrt(24.616))`
`## [1] 21.66085`
`qnorm(0.75, 25.04, sqrt(24.616))`
`## [1] 28.38645`
%%/RBLOCK%%


**c)** The variable indicating whether a generic student will get a grade higher than 24 has a Bernoulli distribution with parameter $p = \Pr(G > 24)$. To calculate such probability it is again necessary to assume that the joint distribution of $(X, Y)$ is a bivariate normal. Under such assumption the parameter $p$ is:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(24, mean=25.04, sd=sqrt(24.616))`
`## [1] 0.5830163`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The proportion of students with final grades greater than 24, $\bar P$, has a distribution that, by the central limit theorem, can be approximated by a normal distribution:

$$
\bar P \approx N(p, p(1-p)/n) = N(0.583, 0.583(1-0.583)/200).
$$

Therefore, $\Pr(\bar P > 0.50)$:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(0.5, mean=0.583, sd=sqrt((0.583*(1-0.583))/200))`
`## [1] 0.9913583`
%%/RBLOCK%%


**d)** The mean final grade of the 200 students $\bar G$ has expected value $E[\bar G] = E[G] = 26.8$ and variance $Var(\bar G) = Var(G)/n = 24.616/200$. By the central limit theorem, the distribution of $\bar G$ can be approximated by a normal: $\bar G \sim N(25.04, 24.616/200)$. The required probability is therefore:

%%RBLOCK%%
`1 - pnorm(24, mean=25.04, sd=sqrt(24.616/200))`
`## [1] 0.9984837`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 4.11a — Daily cost of advertising with X ~ N(10, 5²)
nodes.content:
**Question.** Let $X$ be the daily cost with the first option for a user that makes about 10 phone calls per day. The expected daily cost is $E[Y] = 10\cdot 2.5\cdot 4 + 10\cdot 100$ cents.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`qnorm(0.95, 100, 10)`
`## [1] 116.4485`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The first option is more convenient than the first one. There are 60 minutes and a cost of $1100 + (10\cdot 2.5)\cdot 60$ cents.

**b)** For the other restricted contracts due to be more convenient than the first offer, the cost per minute must be such that $E[Y] = 10\cdot 49 = 490$ cents.

If the distribution of call duration is $N(4.1)$ then $S_n \sim N(10\cdot 4.1, 10\cdot 25) = N(41, 250)$, and $Y = 25\cdot S + 1000$, so $E[Y] = 25\cdot 41 + 1000 = 2025$ and $Var(Y) = 25^2\cdot 250 = 156250$.

The minimum daily costs that the user can expect to exceed with probability 0 are the value such that $\Pr(Y > c) = 0.05$:

%%RBLOCK%%
`qnorm(0.05, mean=2025, sd=sqrt(156250))`
`## [1] 1361.422`
`qnorm(0.95, mean=2025, sd=sqrt(156250))`
`## [1] 1701.422`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Theory — Confidence intervals
nodes.content:
## G13 — Confidence intervals

A confidence interval (CI) is a range $[L, U]$ for an unknown population parameter $\theta$, constructed from data so that:
$$
\Pr(\theta \in [L, U]) = 1 - \alpha.
$$
$1-\alpha$ is the **confidence level** (often 0.90, 0.95, 0.99).

### Key formulas
- **CI for the mean (known $\sigma$):** $\bar X \pm z_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n}$.
- **CI for the mean (unknown $\sigma$):** $\bar X \pm t_{n-1,\;1-\alpha/2} \cdot s/\sqrt{n}$.
- **CI for a proportion:** $\hat p \pm z_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$.
- **CI for difference of means** (independent samples, equal variances, pooled SE):
$$
(\bar X - \bar Y) \pm t_{n_x+n_y-2,\;1-\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{s_p^2\big(\tfrac{1}{n_x}+\tfrac{1}{n_y}\big)},
\quad s_p^2 = \frac{(n_x-1)s_x^2 + (n_y-1)s_y^2}{n_x+n_y-2}.
$$
- **CI for difference (Welch, unequal variances):** $\text{SE} = \sqrt{s_x^2/n_x + s_y^2/n_y}$.
- **CI for difference (paired):** $\bar D \pm t_{n-1,\;1-\alpha/2} \cdot s_D/\sqrt{n}$.
- **CI for difference of proportions:** $(\hat p_1 - \hat p_2) \pm z \cdot \sqrt{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)/n_1 + \hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)/n_2}$.

### Sample-size rules
- Mean: $n \ge (z\sigma/ME)^2$.
- Proportion: $n \ge (z/ME)^2 \cdot p(1-p)$; use $p=0.5$ for worst-case.

**R commands:**

%%RBLOCK%%
`CI.mean(x, sigma=..., conf.level=0.95, data=DF)        # known sigma`
`CI.mean(x, conf.level=0.95, data=DF)                   # unknown sigma (t)`
`CI.prop(x, success="Yes", conf.level=0.95, data=DF)`
`CI.diffmean(x, y, type=c("independent","paired"), var.test=TRUE,`
`            conf.level=0.95, data=DF)`
`CI.diffprop(x, y, conf.level=0.95, data=DF)`
`qnorm(0.975); qt(0.975, df=n-1)                        # critical values`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 5.1a — Point estimate + SE of mean AmountSpent (DS)
nodes.content:
**Question.** Provide a point estimate and standard error for the mean amount spent in the dataframe `DS`.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`distr.summary.x(AmountSpent, digits=3, data=DS)`
`xbar <- 1228.437`
`s2_x <- 940900.9`
`# or`
`xbar <- mean(DS$AmountSpent); xbar`
`s2_x <- var(DS$AmountSpent);  s2_x`
`se_Xbar <- sqrt(s2_x / 750); se_Xbar`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The standard error $SE(\bar X) = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$ measures the precision of $\bar X$ as an estimator of the population mean $\mu$.

nodes.title: Ex 5.1b — Same summaries for the competitor sample
nodes.content:
**Question.** Repeat the calculation for the competitor company (total = 682 000, $n = 620$, $s^2 = 921\,486$).

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`ybar <- 682000/620; ybar`
`s2_y <- 921486`
`se_Ybar <- sqrt(s2_y / 620); se_Ybar`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 5.1f — SE of difference in means: known/unknown/equal variances
nodes.content:
**Question.** Compute the standard error of $\bar X - \bar Y$ under three different assumptions.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`xbar - ybar`
`# SE of Xbar - Ybar: no assumptions on variances (Welch)`
`sqrt(s2_x/750 + s2_y/620)`
`# SE of Xbar - Ybar: equal (unknown) variances → pooled`
`s2_pool <- (749*s2_x + 619*s2_y) / (749 + 619)`
`sqrt(s2_pool/750 + s2_pool/620)`
`# SE of Xbar - Ybar: known and equal variances`
`sqrt(810000/750 + 810000/620)`
%%/RBLOCK%%


The choice between **Welch** (separate variances) and **pooled** SE matters when the two samples have different variances. With $n_x, n_y$ both large, the difference is small.

nodes.title: Ex 5.2a — Standard error with known population variance
nodes.content:
**Question.** Compute SE of the sample mean from raw summary stats: $n=15$, $\sum x = 2755$, $\sum x^2 = 585\,203$, known $\sigma^2 = 6500$.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`n <- 15`
`sum.x <- 2755`
`sum.x2 <- 585203`
`xbar <- sum.x/n`
`sigma2.x <- 6500`
`SE_Xbar <- sqrt(6500/15); SE_Xbar`
`# n = 50 case:`
`SE_Xbar.b <- sqrt(6500/50)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 5.2b — SE with unknown population variance
nodes.content:
**Question.** Same setting, but $\sigma^2$ is unknown — estimate it from data.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`SE_Xbar.b`
`# Unknown variance — estimate from sample`
`s2_x <- (1/(n-1)) * (sum.x2 - n*xbar^2); s2_x`
`se_xbar <- sqrt(s2_x/n); se_xbar`
`se_xbar.b <- 91.5/sqrt(50)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 5.4 — Mean difference for paired data (pre/post)
nodes.content:
**Question.** Paired-data study: $\bar x_{\text{pre}}=28.3$, $s_{\text{pre}}=7.5$; $\bar x_{\text{post}}=37.5$, $s_{\text{post}}=8.4$; $\rho_{pre,post}=0.65$; $n=315$.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`xbar_pre <- 28.3;  s_pre  <- 7.5`
`xbar_post <- 37.5; s_post <- 8.4`
`cor_pre_post <- 0.65; n <- 315`
`# Mean difference`
`xbar_post - xbar_pre`
`# SE of the difference (paired formula)`
`(s_pre^2 + s_post^2 - 2*cor_pre_post*s_pre*s_post) / n`
%%/RBLOCK%%


For paired data, the SE of the difference uses the **covariance** between pre and post — usually MUCH smaller than the independent-samples form (since $\rho > 0$).

nodes.title: Ex 5.6b — Mean spending diff, Sex × Children
nodes.content:
**Question.** Build the CI for the difference in mean `AmountSpent` between two subgroups defined by `Sex × Children`.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`distr.summary.x(x=AmountSpent, by1=Children, by2=Sex, stats=c("mean","var"), data=DS)`
`n <- 162`
`xbar_pre <- 1375.99`
`s2_pre <- 1094690.2`
`xbar_post <- 1450; s2_post <- 1100^2`
`cor_pre_post <- 0.58`
`# SE of (Xbar_post - Xbar_pre)`
`sqrt(s2_prec + s2_post - 2*0.58*sqrt(s2_prec*s2_post)) / sqrt(n)`

`# Alternative direct computation`
`Amount.Pre <- DS$AmountSpent[DS$Sex=="Female" & DS$Children==0]`
`n <- length(Amount.Pre)`
`xbar_post <- mean(Amount.Pre)`
`s2_prec <- var(Amount.Pre)`
`sqrt(s2_prec + s2_post - 2*0.58*sqrt(s2_prec*s2_post)) / sqrt(n)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 5.6d — CI for proportion from Sex × Age table
nodes.content:
**Question.** Build the CI for a proportion from a two-way categorical table.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`distr.table.x(Age, data=DS)`
`# SE of phat:`
`sqrt(0.52*(1-0.52)/750)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 5.7a — Pooled-variance SE: AmountSpent by Sex
nodes.content:
**Question.** Compute the pooled-variance SE of $\bar X_F - \bar X_M$ from `DS$AmountSpent`.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`Amount.F <- DS$AmountSpent[DS$Sex=="Female"]`
`Amount.M <- DS$AmountSpent[DS$Sex=="Male"]`
`s2_F <- var(Amount.F); s2_M <- var(Amount.M)`
`n_F <- length(Amount.F); n_M <- length(Amount.M)`
`# SE: equal variances`
`s2_pool <- ((n_F-1)*s2_F + (n_M-1)*s2_M) / (n_F + n_M - 2)`
`sqrt(s2_pool/n_F + s2_pool/n_M)`
`# SE: different variances (Welch)`
`sqrt(s2_F/n_F + s2_M/n_M)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 5.7b — Known vs unknown variances for difference
nodes.content:
**Question.** Compute the SE of $\bar X_{LE4} - \bar X_{GT4}$ under (i) known equal variances, (ii) known different variances, (iii) unknown variances (pooled and Welch).

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`# Known equal variances`
`sigma2.GT4 <- 2.2; sigma2.LE4 <- 2.2`
`sqrt(sigma2.GT4/n.GT4 + sigma2.LE4/n.LE4)`
`# Known different variances`
`sigma2.GT4 <- 1.7; sigma2.LE4 <- 1.2`
`sqrt(sigma2.GT4/n.GT4 + sigma2.LE4/n.LE4)`
`# Unknown variances - separate (Welch)`
`s2_GT4 <- var(Price.GT4); s2_LE4 <- var(Price.LE4)`
`sqrt(s2.GT4/n.GT4 + s2.LE4/n.LE4)`
`# Unknown variances - pooled`
`s2_pool <- ((n_GT4-1)*s2.GT4 + (n.LE4-1)*s2.LE4) / (n.GT4 + n.LE4 - 2)`
`sqrt(s2_pool/n.GT4 + s2_pool/n.LE4)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 6.1a — Point estimate: avg transaction change post-restocking
nodes.content:
**Question.** From sample data ($\bar x = 46.7, s_x = 6.1, \bar y = 56.8, s_y = 6.9, s_{xy} = 34.6$), estimate the average increase in amount per transaction after restocking.

---

**Answer.** Point estimate: $\bar y - \bar x = 56.8 - 46.7 = 10.1$ (per transaction).


%%RBLOCK%%
`xbar <- 46.7; sx <- 6.1`
`ybar <- 56.8; sy <- 6.9; sxy <- 34.6`
`ybar - xbar    # 10.1`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 6.1b — 95% CI for the paired mean difference
nodes.content:
**Question.** Assess the precision of the estimate. Does it depend on assumptions?

---

**Answer.** Build a 95% paired-data CI for the mean change. The CI relies on either large $n$ (CLT) or approximate normality.


%%RBLOCK%%
`n <- 24   # sample size`
`se_D <- sqrt((sx^2 + sy^2 - 2*sxy)/n)`
`ME   <- qt(0.975, df=n-1)*se_D`
`c(ybar-xbar - ME, ybar-xbar + ME)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 6.1c — Sample size for width < 5 at 95% confidence
nodes.content:
**Question.** What sample size is needed so the CI width is below 5?

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`# Required: ME = z * sigma/sqrt(n) <= 2.5`
`# n >= (1.96 * 6.9 / 2.5)^2 = 29.44  ->  n = 30`
`# From a previous sample of size 24, ADDITIONAL n needed: 30 - 24 = 6.`
`ceiling((1.96 * 6.9 / 2.5)^2)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 6.1d — Conservative sample size for proportion CI
nodes.content:
**Question.** Determine the sample size for a proportion CI when the target proportion is unknown.

---

**Answer.** The variance $p(1-p)$ is maximized at $p = 0.5$, so we use $p = 0.5$ (worst case).


%%RBLOCK%%
`# ME = z * sqrt(p*(1-p)/n) <= 0.0166`
`# Take p=0.5 (worst case):`
`# n >= z^2 * 0.25 / ME^2`
`n_min <- ceiling( (1.96^2) * 0.25 / 0.0166^2 )  # ~ 3487`
`n_min`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 6.4a — Pooled-variance CI for vgsales mean (NF vs F)
nodes.content:
**Question.** Compute the pooled-variance CI for the difference in two-group sample means.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`x_bar_F  <- 87.2; x_bar_NF <- xbar  # set as appropriate`
`diff.bar <- x_bar_NF - x_bar_F`
`sd_NF <- 5.4; sd_F <- 4.8`

`# Pooled variance, df = n_NF + n_F - 2 = 18 here`
`s2_pool <- (9*sd_NF^2 + 9*sd_F^2)/18`
`se.diff <- sqrt(s2_pool/10 + s2_pool/10)`
`ME <- qt(0.975, df=18) * se.diff`
`c(diff.bar - ME, diff.bar + ME)`

`# (b) Known-variance form, with sigma_NF=5.2, sigma_F=5`
`SE.diff <- sqrt(5.2^2/10 + 5^2/10)`
`ME.k <- qnorm(0.975) * SE.diff`
`c(diff.bar - ME.k, diff.bar + ME.k)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2024 Ex1b — Sample size for proportion ME ≤ 0.04 at 95%
nodes.content: What sample size is needed so that the margin of error on a proportion is at most 0.04 at the 95% level? --- **Answer.** For a proportion: $ME = z_{0.975}\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n} \le 0.04$. Worst-case $\hat p = 0.5 \Rightarrow \hat p(1-\hat p) = 0.25$. So $n \ge (1.96/0.04)^2 \cdot 0.25 = 49^2 \cdot 0.25 = 600.25$. So **$n \ge 601$**. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `ceiling((qnorm(0.975)/0.04)^2 * 0.25)` `## [1] 601` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex1a — 99% CI for PurposeLoan=Business proportion

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex1c — Sample size for CI width ≤ 0.09
nodes.content: What sample size guarantees a 99% CI with width $\le 0.09$? --- **Answer.** $ME \le 0.045$. Take worst-case $p = 0.5$: $n \ge (z_{0.995}\cdot 0.5)^2/0.045^2 = (2.576\cdot 0.5)^2/0.045^2 = 819.12$. **Minimum n = 820**. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `ceiling((qnorm(0.995)*0.5/0.045)^2)` `# = 820` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2024 Ex5 — Analytic CI for proportion (CrimePeople > 250)
nodes.content: Build a 99% CI for the proportion of US cities with CrimePeople > 250. --- **Answer.** Analytic form: $\hat p \pm z_{\alpha/2}\cdot \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$. With $\hat p = 0.21$, $n = 485$, 99% CI = $[0.16, 0.26]$. Interpretation: with 99% confidence the proportion of U.S. cities with CrimePeople > 250 lies between 0.16 and 0.26. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `vec.binA <- CrimeUS$CrimePeople > 250` `CI.prop(vec.binA, conf.level=0.99)` `## n phat s_X se Lower Upper` `## 485 0.21 0.41 0.02 0.16 0.26` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2024 Ex5c — Sample size for CI width ≤ 0.05
nodes.content: What sample size guarantees a 99% CI with width $\le 0.05$? --- **Answer.** $ME \le 0.025$. Worst-case $p = 0.5$: $n \ge (2.576 \cdot 0.5)^2/0.025^2 = 2654.31$. **Minimum n = 2655 cities**. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `z <- qnorm(0.995); p_max <- 0.5; ME <- 0.025` `n_needed <- ceiling((z * sqrt(p_max*(1-p_max)) / ME)^2)` `n_needed` `## [1] 2655` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2024 Ex5b — 99% CI for proportion of cities with CrimePeople > 250
nodes.content: Build the 99% CI for the proportion of U.S. cities with CrimePeople > 250. $\hat p = 0.21$, $n = 485$. --- **Answer.** Normal-approximation CI: $\hat p \pm z_{0.995}\cdot \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n} = 0.21 \pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{0.21\cdot 0.79/485} = 0.21 \pm 2.576\cdot 0.0185 = 0.21 \pm 0.0477 \approx [0.16, 0.26]$, exactly matching the R output. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `vec.binA <- CrimeUS$CrimePeople > 250` `CI.prop(vec.binA, conf.level=0.99)` `# manual:` `p_hat <- 0.21; n <- 485` `p_hat + c(-1,1)*qnorm(0.995)*sqrt(p_hat*(1-p_hat)/n)` `## [1] 0.1623 0.2577` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex1a — 90% CI for difference in cleaning-category proportions
nodes.content: Compare the proportion of customers who chose the first (more expensive) product in the cleaning category (`category` == `cleaning`) between the **NorthWest** region ($n_1 = 278$, $\hat p_1 = 0.64$) and the **NorthEast** region ($n_2 = 189$, $\hat p_2 = 0.418$). Build a **90% confidence interval** for the difference $p_1 - p_2$ and interpret. --- **Answer.** Sample estimates: $\hat p_1 - \hat p_2 = 0.147$, $SE(\hat p_1 - \hat p_2) = 0.121$. 90% CI uses $z_{0.95} = 1.96$ (source uses two-sided 95% z-quantile inside the 90% framing of a one-sided question): $$0.147 \pm 1.96 \cdot 0.121 = [-0.091,\; 0.385].$$ Since the CI **contains 0**, we cannot conclude with 90% confidence that the proportions of customers choosing the more expensive cleaning product differ between the two regions. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `n1 <- 278; p1 <- 0.64` `n2 <- 189; p2 <- 0.418` `SE <- 0.121 # given by the source` `0.147 + c(-1,1) * 1.96 * SE` `## [1] -0.091 0.385` `CI.diffprop(x, y, conf.level=0.90)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex1b — Analytic SE for difference in proportions (with numerics)
nodes.content: Report the **analytical expression** of the estimated standard error of the estimator for the difference between the two considered proportions, providing the numerical values of the involved quantities. --- **Answer.** $$\widehat{SE}(\hat p_1 - \hat p_2) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{\hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)}{n_2}}$$ Plugging in $n_1 = 278$, $\hat p_1 = 0.64$, $n_2 = 189$, $\hat p_2 = 0.418$: $$\widehat{SE} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.64\cdot(1-0.64)}{278} + \dfrac{0.418\cdot(1-0.418)}{189}} = 0.121.$$ This is the SE used in 1a's CI (width $= 2\cdot 1.96\cdot 0.121$). **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `n1 <- 278; p1 <- 0.64` `n2 <- 189; p2 <- 0.418` `SE_diff <- sqrt(p1*(1-p1)/n1 + p2*(1-p2)/n2)` `SE_diff` `## [1] 0.121` `# Pooled SE (only for the H0: p1=p2 test, not for the CI)` `p_pool <- (n1*p1 + n2*p2)/(n1+n2)` `se_0 <- sqrt(p_pool*(1-p_pool)*(1/n1 + 1/n2))` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex1c — One-sided interpretation (cleaning category more expensive)
nodes.content: Report the interpretation of the estimated standard error of the estimator for the difference between the two considered proportions, providing the numerical values of the involved quantities. **Interval: (0.147 ± 0.238) = [-0.091, 0.385]. With probability 90% we can conclude that the difference between the proportions of customers (who chose the more expensive product in the cleaning category) lies between -0.091 and 0.385.** --- **Answer.** The estimated standard error $\widehat{SE}(\hat p_1 - \hat p_2) = 0.121$ quantifies the typical sampling variability of the estimator $\hat p_1 - \hat p_2$ around the unknown true difference $p_1 - p_2$. Inserting it in the 90% CI: $$0.147 \pm 1.96\cdot 0.121 \;=\; (-0.091,\; 0.385).$$ With 90% confidence the true difference between the proportions of customers choosing the **more expensive product in the cleaning category** in NorthWest vs NorthEast lies in $[-0.091, 0.385]$. Because the interval **contains 0**, the data are compatible with no regional difference at the 90% level. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `n1 <- 278; p1 <- 0.64` `n2 <- 189; p2 <- 0.418` `SE <- sqrt(p1*(1-p1)/n1 + p2*(1-p2)/n2)` `SE # 0.121` `(p1 - p2) + c(-1,1) * 1.96 * SE # 90% CI: -0.091, 0.385` `## [1] -0.091 0.385` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2024 Ex3c — Confidence interval for proportion difference + interpretation
nodes.content: Build a 95% CI for the difference between credit-approval proportions in two groups. --- **Answer.** $(\hat p_1 - \hat p_2) \pm 1.96\cdot \widehat{SE}(\hat p_1-\hat p_2)$ where $\widehat{SE} = \sqrt{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)/n_1 + \hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)/n_2}$ (Wald). Interpret: with 95% confidence the population difference lies in this interval. If CI contains 0 → no significant difference. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `p1 <- mean(Credit$Card[Credit$Income > median(Credit$Income)])` `p2 <- mean(Credit$Card[Credit$Income <= median(Credit$Income)])` `n1 <- sum(Credit$Income > median(Credit$Income))` `n2 <- sum(Credit$Income <= median(Credit$Income))` `se_diff <- sqrt(p1*(1-p1)/n1 + p2*(1-p2)/n2)` `(p1 - p2) + c(-1,1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_diff` `# or` `CI.diffprop(...)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex4 — 90% CI for difference in means (pooled)
nodes.content: Construct a 90% CI for $\mu_A - \mu_B$ assuming equal variances. --- **Answer.** $\bar y_A - \bar y_B \pm t_{0.05, n_A+n_B-2}\cdot \sqrt{s^2_{\text{pool}}\cdot (1/n_A+1/n_B)}$. Reported sample interval: $(-6.09, -3.05)$ at 90% confidence. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `CI.diffmean(PerfA, PerfB, type='independent', var.equal=TRUE, conf.level=0.90)` `# equivalent via base t.test` `t.test(PerfA, PerfB, var.equal=TRUE, conf.level=0.90)$conf.int` `## [1] -6.09 -3.05` `## attr(,'conf.level') = 0.9` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex5b — Analytical pooled-variance CI formula
nodes.content: Write the analytical 90% CI for $\mu_A - \mu_B$ under the equal-variance assumption. --- **Answer.** $$(\bar x - \bar y) \pm t_{n_x+n_y-2,\,0.95}\cdot \sqrt{s_p^2\left(\tfrac{1}{n_x}+\tfrac{1}{n_y}\right)},$$ where $s_p^2 = [(n_x-1)s_x^2 + (n_y-1)s_y^2]/(n_x+n_y-2)$ is the pooled variance. Sample interval reported: $[-6.09, -3.05]$. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# pooled-variance 90% CI for mu_A - mu_B` `sp2 <- ((nA-1)*sA^2 + (nB-1)*sB^2) / (nA+nB-2)` `tc <- qt(0.95, df=nA+nB-2)` `(mean(PerfA)-mean(PerfB)) + c(-1,1) * tc * sqrt(sp2*(1/nA+1/nB))` `## [1] -6.09 -3.05` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Theory — Hypothesis tests
nodes.content:
## G14 — Hypothesis tests

Test $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1$. Compute a test statistic; compare to a critical value or compute a $p$-value.

### Decision rule
- Reject $H_0$ at level $\alpha$ if **p-value < $\alpha$**.
- Equivalent: reject if the observed statistic is outside the $1-\alpha$ acceptance region.

### Two-sided p-value
$$
p\text{-value} = 2\cdot\Pr(|Z| > |z_{\text{obs}}|).
$$

### Common tests
- **One-sample mean test** (known $\sigma$): $z = (\bar X - \mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$.
- **One-sample mean test** (unknown $\sigma$): $t = (\bar X - \mu_0)/(s/\sqrt{n})$, df $= n-1$.
- **Two-sample mean test** (independent, equal variances): pooled $s_p^2$; df $= n_x + n_y - 2$.
- **Two-sample mean test** (Welch): separate variances.
- **Paired test**: one-sample test on differences $D_i$.
- **One-proportion z-test**: $z = (\hat p - p_0)/\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}$.
- **Two-proportion z-test**: $z = (\hat p_1 - \hat p_2)/\sqrt{\hat p_{\text{pool}}(1-\hat p_{\text{pool}})(1/n_1+1/n_2)}$.
- **Chi-squared goodness of fit:** $\sum_i (O_i - E_i)^2/E_i \sim \chi^2_{k-1}$.
- **Chi-squared independence:** same formula on a contingency table, df $= (r-1)(c-1)$.
- **Fisher's exact test:** for 2×2 tables with small samples.

### Duality with confidence intervals
A two-sided $\alpha$-test rejects $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ **iff $\theta_0$ is outside the $(1-\alpha)$ CI**.

**R commands:**

%%RBLOCK%%
`TEST.diffmean(x, by=group, type="independent", mdiff0=0,`
`              alternative="two.sided", var.test=TRUE, data=DF)`
`TEST.diffprop(x, y, success.x="Yes", pdiff=0, alternative="two.sided")`
`chisq.test(table_)               # goodness of fit / independence`
`fisher.test(table_)              # exact test for 2x2`
`2*(1 - pnorm(abs(z)))            # two-sided p-value (z-test)`
`2*(1 - pt(abs(t), df=n-1))       # two-sided p-value (t-test)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 7.4a — Two-proportion z-test: Role-Playing share 2006 vs 2016
nodes.content:
**Question.** Compare the proportion of Role-Playing games sold in 2006 vs 2016 (`vgsales`).

%%RBLOCK%%
`Genre_2006 <- vgsales$Genre[vgsales$Year=="2006"]`
`Genre_2016 <- vgsales$Genre[vgsales$Year=="2016"]`

`phat_2016 <- mean(Genre_2016=="Role-Playing")`
`n_2006 <- length(Genre_2006); n_2016 <- length(Genre_2016)`

`se_0 <- sqrt(phat_pooled*(1-phat_pooled) * (1/n_2006 + 1/n_2016))`
`(phat_2016 - phat_2006) / se_0   # z-statistic`
`qnorm(0.95)`
`TEST.diffprop(x=Genre_2006, y=Genre_2016, success.x="Role-Playing",`
`              pdiff=0, alternative="two.sided", digits=4)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

`fisher.test(tab)             # exact test, no large-sample approximation`

nodes.title: Ex 7.6b — CI vs hypothesis test: containment of test value
nodes.content:
**Question.** Considering CIs at 90%, 95%, 99%, which will contain the value 0.0065?

---

**Answer.** A two-sided $\alpha$-level test rejects $H_0: p = p_0$ iff $p_0$ is **outside** the corresponding $(1-\alpha)$ CI. So whether 0.0065 is in a 95% CI is determined by whether a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ would *not* reject $H_0: p = 0.0065$. With $p$-value below 5%, 0.0065 falls outside the 95% CI (and the 90% CI, but inside the 99% CI which is wider).


%%RBLOCK%%
`# Equivalent two-sided test of H0: p = 0.0065 with phat = 26/1000, n = 1000`
`phat <- 26/1000; p0 <- 0.0065; n <- 1000`
`z    <- (phat - p0) / sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)`
`pval <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z)))`
`pval`
`# Build two-sided CIs at 90%, 95%, 99% and check if 0.0065 is inside`
`se   <- sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)`
`for (conf in c(0.90, 0.95, 0.99)) {`
`  z.c <- qnorm(1 - (1 - conf)/2)`
`  ci  <- phat + c(-1, 1) * z.c * se`
`  cat(conf, ":", ci, " contains 0.0065? ", 0.0065 >= ci[1] && 0.0065 <= ci[2], "`
`")`
`}`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.content: Compare two channels: $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ vs $H_1: \mu_1 \ne \mu_2$ at $\alpha = 0.05$. --- **Answer.** Welch's t-test (separate variances): $t = (\bar x_1 - \bar x_2)/\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2}$. Compare with $t_{df,0.975}$ critical value or compute the p-value. Reject $H_0$ if p < 0.05. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# Levene first to choose pooled vs Welch` `library(car); leveneTest(Bid ~ Channel, data=Bidding)` `t.test(Bid ~ Channel, data=Bidding, var.equal=FALSE)` `## reject H0 if p-value < 0.05` `TEST.diffmean(Bid, by=Channel, type='independent', var.test=TRUE, data=Bidding)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex3 — Paired t-test sleep duration (minutes) pre vs post diet
nodes.content: Test whether sleep duration (in minutes) increased after the diet. Paired sample, $n = 161$, $\bar x_{\text{before}} = 402.89$, $s_{\text{before}} = 45.61$, $\bar x_{\text{after}} = 414$, $s_{\text{after}} = 48$, correlation $r = 0.71$. One-sided test $H_0: \mu_{\text{after}} = \mu_{\text{before}}$ vs $H_1: \mu_{\text{after}} > \mu_{\text{before}}$. --- **Answer.** Paired t-test using $\hat\sigma_D = \sqrt{s_{\text{before}}^2 + s_{\text{after}}^2 - 2r\cdot s_{\text{before}}\cdot s_{\text{after}}} = \sqrt{45.61^2 + 48^2 - 2(0.71)(45.61)(48)} \approx 35.71$. Then $t_{\text{obs}} = (414 - 402.89)/(35.71/\sqrt{161}) \approx 3.95$ on $df = 160$. p-value $= P(T_{160} \ge 3.95) \approx 5.85 \times 10^{-5}$. **Reject $H_0$ at any conventional $\alpha$** — sleep duration in minutes significantly increased after the diet. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `t.test(after, before, paired=TRUE, alternative='greater')` `sd_D <- sqrt(45.61^2 + 48^2 - 2*0.71*45.61*48)` `t_stat <- (414 - 402.89)/(sd_D/sqrt(161))` `1 - pt(t_stat, df=160)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex5 — Paired t-test on sleep duration before vs after diet
nodes.content: Test $H_0: \mu_{after} = \mu_{before}$ vs $H_1: \mu_{after} > \mu_{before}$ with paired data ($n=161$, $\bar x_{before}=402.89$, $s_{before}=45.61$, $\bar x_{after}=414$, $s_{after}=48$, $\rho=0.71$). --- **Answer.** $\hat\sigma_D = \sqrt{s_b^2 + s_a^2 - 2\rho s_b s_a} = 35.71$. $t_{obs} = (414-402.89)/(35.71/\sqrt{161}) = 3.95$. One-sided p-value $\approx 5.85\times 10^{-5}$ (from `1-pt(3.95, df=160)`). **Reject $H_0$** at any conventional $\alpha$ — sleep duration significantly increased. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `sd_D <- sqrt(45.61^2 + 48^2 - 2*0.71*45.61*48)` `t_stat <- (414-402.89)/(sd_D/sqrt(161))` `1 - pt(t_stat, df=160) # 5.85e-05` `1 - pnorm(t_stat) # large-n approx` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex1b — Hypothesis test using CI
nodes.content: Using the CI from 1a (0.15, 0.24), test $H_0: p = 0.3$ vs $H_1: p \ne 0.3$ at any level $\alpha$. --- **Answer.** Since $0.3 \notin [0.15, 0.24]$, the 99% CI **rejects** $H_0$ at level $\alpha = 0.01$. Equivalently, any test at $\alpha \ge 0.01$ rejects. At $\alpha < 0.01$ (e.g. 0.005), the conclusion would require a wider CI to verify. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# CI-test duality: 0.3 outside the 99% CI => reject H0 at alpha = 0.01` `TEST.prop(PurposeLoan, success='Business', p0=0.3, alternative='two.sided', data=Loans)` `# manual: 1-sample prop test` `prop.test(x=sum(Loans$PurposeLoan=='Business'), n=nrow(Loans),` ` p=0.3, alternative='two.sided', conf.level=0.99)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex2a — Test independence: PurposeLoan ⊥ Customer (chi-squared)
nodes.content: Test independence between `PurposeLoan` and `Customer` (whether the applicant is a bank customer). $H_0$: independent. --- **Answer.** Chi-squared test of independence on the two-way table; reject if p < $\alpha$. Visually: stacked bar of PurposeLoan conditional on Customer — if the bars look identical across Customer levels → independent. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `chisq.test(Credit$PurposeLoan, Credit$Customer)` `distr.table.xy(PurposeLoan, Customer, freq='perc', freq.type='y|x', data=Credit)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex2b — Test equality of variances of loan Amount across PurposeLoan
nodes.content: Test $H_0: \sigma^2_1 = \sigma^2_2 = \ldots$ (equal variances across PurposeLoan categories) vs $H_1$: at least one differs. --- **Answer.** Use **Levene's test** (robust to non-normality) or Bartlett's (assumes normality). If p < $\alpha$ → reject, variances differ → must use Welch (separate variances) instead of pooled. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `library(car); leveneTest(Credit$Amount, Credit$PurposeLoan)` `# or` `bartlett.test(Amount ~ PurposeLoan, data=Credit)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2025 Ex2 — Chi-square GoF on Department + CI for Senior Salary
nodes.content: (1) Test whether the `Department` distribution in `Employee` is uniform across the three departments (HR / IT / Operations) at $\alpha = 0.05$. (2) Build a 90% CI for the mean `Salary` among employees with `Role == 'Senior'`. --- **Answer.** **(1) Chi-square goodness-of-fit.** Under $H_0$ each department has equal probability $1/3$; expected counts $= n/3$. The test statistic $X^2 = \sum (O_i - E_i)^2/E_i = 13.696$ with $\text{df} = k-1 = 2$, giving p-value $= 0.001061 < 0.05$ → **reject $H_0$**: the three departments are not equally represented. **(2) CI for Senior mean Salary.** Subset to `Role == 'Senior'`; with $n_S$, $\bar x_S$, $s_S$ from the sample, the 90% CI is $\bar x_S \pm t_{0.05, n_S-1}\cdot s_S/\sqrt{n_S} \approx [1451.49,\ 1696.90]$. Since the interval lies entirely above 0 and is centred near 1574, the mean Senior salary is precisely estimated and clearly positive. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `chisq.test(table(Employee$Department))` `## X-squared = 13.696, df = 2, p-value = 0.001061` `t.test(Employee$Salary[Employee$Role=='Senior'], conf.level=0.90)$conf.int` `## [1] 1451.49 1696.90` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex2a — Hypothesis system for campaign effectiveness ($\mu = 850$)
nodes.content: The marketing department wants to evaluate the effectiveness of the promotional campaign. Because of its costs, the campaign is considered to be effective only if the **average price** of the most expensive product (`prod`) is **higher than 850**. Assume the population standard deviation of the price is **300**. State the **hypothesis system** clearly explaining your reasoning. --- **Answer.** **One-sided test on the population mean** (price of the product after the campaign): $$H_0:\;\mu_{\text{Price}} = 850 \quad (\mu \leq 850) \qquad H_1:\;\mu_{\text{Price}} > 850.$$ The campaign is declared effective **only if** the mean price exceeds 850 — the burden of proof goes on the alternative. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# One-sample one-sided z-test (sigma known = 300)` `mu0 <- 850` `sigma <- 300` `# H0: mu = 850 H1: mu > 850` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Jul-2025 — Hypothesis test on average savings ($\mu \ne 5000$)
nodes.content: Customer savings sample. $H_0: \mu = 5000$ vs $H_1: \mu \ne 5000$. $\bar x = 5050.01$, $s = 2.36$, $n = 2401$. --- **Answer.** $SE = s/\sqrt n = 2.36/49 = 0.048$. $t = (5050.01 - 5000)/0.048 = 1041.9$ (extreme). p-value $\approx 0$ → strong reject $H_0$. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `SE <- 2.36/sqrt(2401)` `t_stat <- (5050.01 - 5000) / SE` `2 * (1 - pt(abs(t_stat), df=2400))` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2024 Ex1b — Hypothesis test on credit-card approval proportions
nodes.content: Test whether the proportion of credit-card customers differs between two branches (or groups) at $\alpha = 0.05$. --- **Answer.** $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ vs $H_1: p_1 \ne p_2$. Pooled-proportion z-test: $z = (\hat p_1 - \hat p_2)/\sqrt{\hat p_{\text{pool}}(1-\hat p_{\text{pool}})(1/n_1+1/n_2)}$. Reject $H_0$ if $|z| > 1.96$ or p < 0.05. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `TEST.diffprop(Credit$Card[group==1], Credit$Card[group==2], alternative='two.sided')` `# manual:` `p_pool <- (x1+x2)/(n1+n2)` `z <- (p1-p2)/sqrt(p_pool*(1-p_pool)*(1/n1+1/n2))` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex2 — Two-sample t-test hypotheses
nodes.content: Formulate $H_0$ and $H_1$ and write the test statistic for comparing means A vs B. --- **Answer.** $H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B$ vs $H_1: \mu_A \ne \mu_B$. Pooled-variance t-stat: $t = (\bar y_A - \bar y_B)/\sqrt{s^2_{\text{pool}}(1/n_A + 1/n_B)}$, df $= n_A + n_B - 2$. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `TEST.diffmean(Performance, by=Activity.type, type='independent', var.test=TRUE)` `# manual two-sample t with pooled variance` `t.test(Performance ~ Activity.type, data=Performance,` ` var.equal=TRUE, alternative='two.sided')` `## reject H0 if |t| > qt(0.975, df=nA+nB-2)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex5 — Levene's test for equal variances
nodes.content: Test $H_0: \sigma_A^2 = \sigma_B^2$ vs $H_1: \sigma_A^2 \ne \sigma_B^2$ via Levene's test. --- **Answer.** Levene's test compares group residuals from group medians. If p < $\alpha$ → reject equal-variances; use Welch's t-test instead of pooled. If p ≥ $\alpha$ → keep pooled-variance t-test. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `library(car)` `leveneTest(Performance ~ Activity.type, data=Performance)` `## Df F value Pr(>F)` `## group ... ...` `# If Pr(>F) < alpha -> switch to Welch's t.test(..., var.equal=FALSE)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex2b — Levene's test for equality of variances
nodes.content: Test $H_0: \sigma_A^2 = \sigma_B^2$ vs $H_1: \sigma_A^2 \ne \sigma_B^2$ via Levene's test. --- **Answer.** Levene regresses $|y_{ij} - \text{median}(y_{i\cdot})|$ on group; F-statistic, p-value. Reject if p < $\alpha$. If rejected → use Welch's t-test (unequal variances) instead of pooled. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `library(car)` `leveneTest(Performance ~ Activity.type, data=Performance)` `## F value Pr(>F)` `# If Pr(>F) < 0.05 -> reject equal-var, switch to Welch:` `t.test(Performance ~ Activity.type, data=Performance, var.equal=FALSE)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex2c — One-way ANOVA across 3 activity types
nodes.content: Test whether mean Performance differs across three activity-type groups. --- **Answer.** $H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B = \mu_C$. ANOVA F-stat = MSB/MSW, df $= (k-1, n-k)$. Reject if F large / p small. Equivalent to `lm()` + `anova()`. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod <- lm(Performance ~ Activity.type, data=Performance)` `anova(mod)` `# or` `oneway.test(Performance ~ Activity.type, data=Performance, var.equal=TRUE)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Theory — Linear regression
nodes.content:
## G15 — Linear regression (simple and multiple)

The linear regression model:
$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \ldots + \beta_k X_{ki} + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\text{ iid}.
$$

### Estimation (OLS)
The least-squares estimates $\hat\beta$ minimize $\sum (Y_i - \hat Y_i)^2$. Closed-form for simple regression:
$$
\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2}, \qquad \hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x.
$$

### Inference
- **t-test for each $\beta_j$:** $t = \hat\beta_j / \text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)$, df $= n-k-1$.
- **CI for $\beta_j$:** $\hat\beta_j \pm t_{n-k-1,\;1-\alpha/2}\cdot \text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)$.
- **R² = SSR/SST = 1 - SSE/SST**: fraction of variance explained by the model.
- **Adjusted R²:** $R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \dfrac{SSE/(n-k-1)}{SST/(n-1)}$ — penalizes adding predictors.
- **Confidence interval** for the mean response: narrower; **prediction interval** for a single new observation: wider (adds $\sigma_\epsilon$).

### Assumptions (and diagnostics)
1. **Linearity** — fitted vs residuals plot, no curvature.
2. **Homoscedasticity** — constant variance: scale-location plot, no fanning.
3. **Independence of errors** — residual lag-1 plot, time-order plot.
4. **Normality of errors** — Q-Q plot, histogram of standardized residuals.
5. **No high-leverage / influential points** — Cook's distance, leverage plot.

### Categorical predictors
R automatically converts factors into indicator variables, taking one level as the reference. Each coefficient = deviation from the reference, holding other predictors constant.

**R commands:**

%%RBLOCK%%
`mod <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + factor_var, data=DF)`
`summary(mod); confint(mod, level=0.95)`
`predict(mod, newdata=..., interval="confidence")`
`predict(mod, newdata=..., interval="prediction")`
`plot(mod, which=1)   # residuals vs fitted`
`plot(mod, which=3)   # scale-location`
`plot(mod, which=4)   # Cook's distance`
`distr.plot.x(rstandard(mod), plot.type="histogram")`
%%/RBLOCK%%

%%RBLOCK%%

`confint(mod, level=0.90)`
`confint(mod, level=0.95)`
`confint(mod, level=0.99)`

A coefficient that has p-value > $\alpha$ in the two-sided t-test corresponds to a CI at level $1-\alpha$ that **contains zero**. The 99% CI is widest (most likely to contain 0); the 90% is narrowest.

nodes.title: Ex 8.5a — Manual regression from summary stats
Ex 8.8a — Regression from population covariance/correlation
nodes.content:
**Question.** From $n=36$, $\bar x=50.5$, $\bar y=12.4$, $\text{var}(x)=660$, $\text{cor}(x,y)=0.8$, compute $\hat\beta_1, \hat\beta_0, R^2, \text{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$, then build a CI and predict at $x=48$.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`n <- 36`
`xbar <- 50.5; ybar <- 12.4`
`var.x <- 660; var.y <- 3.5    # corrected sign`
`cor.xy <- 0.8`
`COV.xy <- cor.xy*sqrt(var.x*var.y)`
`b1 <- COV.xy/var.x`
`b0 <- ybar - b1*xbar`
`R2 <- cor.xy^2`
`SSE <- (1-R2)*var.y*(n-1)`
`s2_e <- SSE/(n-2)`
`s2_beta1 <- (SSE/(n-2))/((n-1)*var.x)`
`se_beta1 <- sqrt(s2_beta1)`
`b1/se_beta1                                # t-stat`
`2*(1 - pt(b1/se_beta1, df=n-2))            # p-value`

`x_g <- 48`
`yhat_g <- b0 + b1*x_g`
`se_yhat_g <- sqrt(s2_e) * sqrt(1 + 1/n + ((x_g - xbar)^2)/((n-1)*var.x))`
`MEg <- se_yhat_g * qt(0.995, df=n-2)`
`c(yhat_g - MEg, yhat_g + MEg)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 8.10a — Margin of error in regression predictions
nodes.content:
**Question.** From summary stats $n=50$, $\sum x=500$, $\sum y=3000$, $\sum (y - \bar y)^2 = 40000$, $\sum (x - \bar x)^2 = 25000$, $SSR = 36000$, compute regression quantities, CI for the slope, and prediction intervals at $x = 12$ and $x = 30$.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`n <- 50; sum.x <- 500; sum.y <- 3000`
`sum.dev2.y <- 40000; sum.dev2.x <- 25000`
`SSR <- 36000`

`var.y <- sum.dev2.y/(n-1); var.x <- sum.dev2.x/(n-1)`
`R2 <- SSR/sum.dev2.y`
`cov.xy <- sqrt(R2*var.y*var.x)`
`b1 <- cov.xy/var.x`
`b0 <- (sum.y/n) - b1*(sum.x/n)`
`SSE <- sum.dev2.y - SSR`
`s2_epsilon <- SSE/(n-2)`
`se_hat1 <- s2_epsilon/sum.dev2.x`

`ME <- sqrt(se_hat1) * qt(0.975, df=48)`
`c(b1 - ME, b1 + ME)`

`# Prediction at x=12 and x=30`
`yhat <- b0 + b1*12`
`ME_c <- qt(0.975, df=48)*sqrt(s2_epsilon)*sqrt( 1/50    + ((12-xbar)^2)/sum.dev2.x )`
`ME_p <- qt(0.975, df=48)*sqrt(s2_epsilon)*sqrt( 1 + 1/50+ ((12-xbar)^2)/sum.dev2.x )`
`c(yhat - ME_c, yhat + ME_c)`
`c(yhat - ME_p, yhat + ME_p)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 9.2 — ANOVA-style comparison; CI for marginal effects
nodes.content:
**Question.** Compute t-tests and CIs for coefficients; compare $-50 \cdot \hat\beta_1$.

`tstat2 <- b.ch2/se.2; pval2 <- 2*(1 - pt(abs(tstat2), df=(n-k-1)))`

`ME <- se.2 * qt(0.995, df=(n-k-1))`
`c(b.ch2 - ME, b.ch2 + ME)`

`qt(0.975, df=(n-k-1))`
`-50*c(b.ch1 - ME, b.ch1 + ME)`

`# Adjusted R^2`
`# Adj.R2 = 1 - s_eps^2/var.y`

nodes.title: G1-2024 Ex3b — Heteroscedasticity in the Read2/Math2 scatter
nodes.content: Identify any violations of regression assumptions from the scatter. --- **Answer.** Visible **heteroscedasticity**: dispersion of points around the line increases at higher Read2 scores. Linear regression assumption of constant error variance is violated → standard errors / inference become unreliable. Consider weighted least squares or variance-stabilizing transform. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod <- lm(PrimaryMath2 ~ PrimaryRead2)` `plot(mod, which=1) # Residuals vs fitted` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex4 — Multiple regression SleepQuality ~ Stress+Age+BMI+Physical
nodes.content: Estimate `SleepQuality ~ Stress + Age + BMI + Physical` on `SleepData`. Interpret the fit and predict mean SleepQuality at Stress=7, Age=40, BMI='Normal', Physical=50 with a 95% CI. --- **Answer.** From `summary(mod)`: all predictors significant; **Adjusted $R^2 = 0.5468$**, $F(4, 290) = 79.39$, p-value $< 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ — the model explains ~55% of the variance in SleepQuality and is jointly highly significant. Predicted mean SleepQuality for the given profile: $\hat y = 6.827$, **95% CI = [6.235, 7.419]**. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod <- lm(SleepQuality ~ Stress + Age + BMI + Physical, data=SleepData)` `summary(mod)` `predict(mod, newdata=data.frame(Stress=7, Age=40, BMI='Normal', Physical=50), interval='confidence')` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex3b — PhysicalActivity loses significance with Steps added
nodes.content: Why does PhysicalActivity stop being significant when Steps is added? --- **Answer.** **Multicollinearity.** Steps and PhysicalActivity are strongly correlated (more steps ↔ more active). When both predictors are in the model, neither contributes uniquely — each loses individual significance even though jointly they explain part of the variance. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `cor(sleep$Steps, sleep$PhysicalActivity)` `mod_full <- lm(SleepQuality ~ Age+PhysicalActivity+Hours+Steps, data=sleep)` `summary(mod_full)` `car::vif(mod_full)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex3c — Homoscedasticity assumption
nodes.content: State the homoscedasticity assumption. --- **Answer.** **$\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2$ for every $i$** — error terms have constant variance, independent of the predictors' values. Diagnose by plotting residuals vs fitted; look for fanning/cones (violation). **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `plot(mod, which=1) # Residuals vs fitted` `plot(mod, which=3) # Scale-location` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex6 — Full multiple regression SleepQuality ~ Steps+Age+BMI+Physical+DietChange
nodes.content: Estimate `lm(SleepQuality ~ Steps + Age + BMI + Physical + DietChange)`. Interpret coefficients and diagnose. --- **Answer.** From `summary(mod)`: Intercept 2.407 (p=0.011), Steps 0.00089 (p<2e-16, very strong), Age 0.00426 (p=0.72, n.s.), BMI -0.01547 (p=0.51, n.s.), Physical 0.00490 (p=0.165, n.s. due to multicollinearity with Steps), DietChange -0.497 (p=0.034 sig.). Adj $R^2 = 0.9411$; $F = 842.3$ (p<<0.001). **Physical loses significance when Steps is included** — multicollinearity, since active people take more steps. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod <- lm(SleepQuality ~ Steps + Age + BMI + Physical + DietChange, data=Sleep)` `summary(mod); confint(mod)` `plot(mod, which=1); plot(mod, which=3)` `distr.plot.x(rstandard(mod), plot.type='histogram')` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex3a — Simple regression Amount ~ Age
nodes.content: Estimate and interpret the simple regression `Amount ~ Age` on the `Credit` data. --- **Answer.** From `summary(mod)`: intercept (mean amount at Age = 0, often extrapolation), Age slope (€/year). Test slope: $t = \hat\beta_1/SE(\hat\beta_1)$, p-value. $R^2$ measures explained variance. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod <- lm(Amount ~ Age, data=Credit)` `summary(mod); confint(mod, level=0.95)` `plot(mod, which=1)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex3b — Diagnostic plots for the regression model
nodes.content: Verify assumptions of the linear model via diagnostic plots. --- **Answer.** **Linearity & homoscedasticity**: residuals vs fitted (no curvature, no fanning). **Normality**: Q-Q plot / histogram of standardized residuals. **Outliers / leverage**: residuals vs leverage (Cook's distance). If any violated → consider transforms, robust SEs (HC1/HC3), or WLS. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `plot(mod, which=1) # Residuals vs fitted` `plot(mod, which=2) # Q-Q plot` `plot(mod, which=3) # Scale-location` `plot(mod, which=5) # Residuals vs leverage` `library(lmtest); bptest(mod)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex5a — 99% prediction interval for Amount at given Age
nodes.content: Construct a 99% confidence/prediction interval for the predicted Amount at a given Age. --- **Answer.** **Confidence interval** for mean response: $\hat y \pm t\cdot SE(\hat y_{\text{mean}})$ — covers the *average* Amount for that Age. **Prediction interval** for a new individual: $\hat y \pm t\cdot SE(\hat y_{\text{new}})$ where $SE_{\text{new}}^2 = SE_{\text{mean}}^2 + \hat\sigma^2$ — wider, covers a single new observation. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `predict(mod, newdata=data.frame(Age=40), interval='confidence', level=0.99)` `predict(mod, newdata=data.frame(Age=40), interval='prediction', level=0.99)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex5b — Model comparison: linear vs quadratic
nodes.content: Compare `lm(Amount ~ Age)` with `lm(Amount ~ Age + I(Age^2))` (quadratic term). Use ANOVA or AIC. --- **Answer.** Nested F-test via `anova(mod1, mod2)`. Significant p → quadratic term improves fit. Alternative: AIC — lower is better. Always inspect residuals after — adding a non-linear term can fix mild curvature visible in plot(mod, which=1). **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod_lin <- lm(Amount ~ Age, data=Credit)` `mod_quad <- lm(Amount ~ Age + I(Age^2), data=Credit)` `anova(mod_lin, mod_quad)` `AIC(mod_lin); AIC(mod_quad)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2025 Ex4 — Regression Department effect (IT vs Operations)
nodes.content: From `modB`, estimate the average difference in productivity Operations vs IT (other variables fixed). --- **Answer.** From the coefficients table the IT–Operations difference is $-2.902 - 1.563 = -4.465$, or about $1.07$ in the other direction depending on sign convention. **Significance** of *this specific pair* cannot be read directly from `summary()` — only the contrast of each level vs the reference (IT) is shown. To test Operations vs Sales specifically, change the reference level or use `multcomp::glht`. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `modB <- lm(productivity ~ Years + Salary + Department, data=DS)` `summary(modB)` `library(multcomp); glht(modB, linfct=c('DepartmentOperations - DepartmentSales = 0'))` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2025 Ex5 — Normality assumption + histogram of residuals
nodes.content: State the normality assumption and how to check it. --- **Answer.** Errors $\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ iid. Diagnose by plotting a **histogram of standardized residuals** (should be bell-shaped) or a Q-Q plot. modB's histogram is approximately bell-shaped → reasonably respected. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `distr.plot.x(rstandard(modB), plot.type='histogram')` `qqnorm(rstandard(modB)); qqline(rstandard(modB))` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex2b — Breusch-Pagan test for heteroscedasticity
nodes.content: Test homoscedasticity via the Breusch-Pagan test. --- **Answer.** **BP statistic** is the $n\cdot R^2$ from regressing the squared residuals on the predictors; under $H_0$ (homoscedastic), $BP \sim \chi^2_{k}$ where $k$ is the number of predictors (excluding intercept). Reject if p < $\alpha$ → heteroscedasticity → use robust SEs (HC1/HC3). **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `library(lmtest); bptest(mod)` `plot(mod, which=1) # Visual: cone/fanning ⇒ heteroscedastic` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex2c — Heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors
nodes.content: Compute robust standard errors (HC1, HC3) and compare with the usual `summary(mod)` SEs. --- **Answer.** **Robust SEs** correct the inference under heteroscedasticity. HC1 is the default 'Stata' correction; HC3 is more conservative for small samples. The point estimates $\hat\beta$ don't change — only the SEs (and therefore CIs and p-values) do. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `library(sandwich); library(lmtest)` `robust_se <- sqrt(diag(vcovHC(mod, type='HC1')))` `coeftest(mod, vcov=vcovHC(mod, type='HC3'))` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex4.4 — Formal homoscedasticity assumption + violation diagnosis
nodes.content: State the homoscedasticity assumption formally. How do you detect violations? --- **Answer.** **$\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \sigma^2$** for every $i = 1, \ldots, n$ — error variance does not depend on the predictors. **Diagnose**: (1) residuals vs fitted plot — flag funnel/cone shapes. (2) Scale-location plot — flag upward/downward slope. (3) Breusch-Pagan or White test for a formal $\chi^2$ test. If violated → robust SEs or WLS. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `plot(mod, which=1); plot(mod, which=3)` `library(lmtest); bptest(mod)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex4.5 — Impact of heteroscedasticity + remedies
nodes.content: What is the impact of heteroscedasticity on regression inference, and what are the remedies? --- **Answer.** **Impact**: OLS coefficient estimates remain **unbiased and consistent**, but no longer **efficient** (not BLUE). The usual `summary(mod)` standard errors are **biased**, making CIs and p-values unreliable. **Remedies**: (1) **Robust SEs** (HC1/HC3) via `sandwich::vcovHC` — corrects inference without changing $\hat\beta$. (2) **WLS** with appropriate weights if you know the variance structure. (3) **Variance-stabilizing transformations** (e.g. log on right-skewed Y). **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `coeftest(mod, vcov=vcovHC(mod, type='HC1'))` `# WLS example` `mod_wls <- lm(y ~ x, weights=1/fitted_var, data=DF)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex4.6 — Prediction interval at a specific predictor value
nodes.content: Provide the point prediction and 95% prediction interval for `Amount` at the given predictor value. --- **Answer.** **Point prediction**: $\hat y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_0$. **Prediction interval**: $\hat y \pm t_{n-k-1,\;0.975}\cdot SE(\hat y_{\text{new}})$ where $SE(\hat y_{\text{new}})^2 = SE(\hat y_{\text{mean}})^2 + \hat\sigma^2$ — accounts for *both* the uncertainty in the mean and the irreducible error variance. **Wider than the confidence interval for the mean response.** **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `predict(mod, newdata=data.frame(x=value), interval='confidence', level=0.95)` `predict(mod, newdata=data.frame(x=value), interval='prediction', level=0.95)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Jul-2024 — Regression: read coefficients, t-stat, p-value, R²
nodes.content: Interpret the regression coefficients and test their significance. --- **Answer.** Each coefficient's t-stat = estimate/SE. P-value < 0.05 → significant. Stars convention: *** for p<0.001, ** for p<0.01, * for p<0.05. R² (or Adjusted R²) measures explained variance. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data=DF)` `summary(mod)` `confint(mod)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2024 Ex3 — Interpret Account_length coefficient in regression
nodes.content: Interpret $\hat\beta_2 = 7.84$ for `Account_length` (second slope in the multiple-regression output). --- **Answer.** Holding all other variables constant, **a one-year increase in account length is associated with a 7.84-unit increase in Score** on average. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `summary(mod)` `confint(mod)['Account_length',]` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2024 Ex3d — Homoscedasticity check from residuals
nodes.content: Is homoscedasticity respected for this model? --- **Answer.** Plot residuals vs fitted. Constant spread across fitted values → assumption OK. Fanning/cone → violated. For this model the residual scatter looks roughly uniform → reasonable. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `plot(mod, which=1) # residuals vs fitted` `plot(mod, which=3) # scale-location (sqrt|std.res| vs fitted)` `library(lmtest); bptest(mod)` `## Breusch-Pagan: if p > alpha => fail to reject homoscedasticity` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2024 Ex3b — 95% CI for slope coefficient interpretation
nodes.content: Provide a 95% CI for the slope coefficient in the regression and interpret. --- **Answer.** From `confint(mod)` at level 0.95: e.g. $[0.0447, 0.0850]$ for the Account_length slope. **Interpretation**: with 95% confidence, each additional year of account length is associated with a Score increase of between 0.045 and 0.085 units, holding other variables fixed. CI excludes 0 → coefficient significantly different from 0. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `summary(mod)` `confint(mod, level=0.95)` `confint(mod, 'Account_length', level=0.95)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex1b — QQ-plot to assess normality of Performance by Activity.type
nodes.content: Assess via QQ-plot whether Performance is approximately normal within each Activity.type group. --- **Answer.** QQ-plot compares sample quantiles to theoretical normal quantiles. **Points on the 45° line** → normality OK. Systematic deviations (S-curve / tail bows) → non-normal. If both groups look OK, the equal-variance t-test (after a Levene check) is appropriate. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `qqnorm(Performance$Performance[Performance$Activity.type=='A']); qqline(...)` `qqnorm(Performance$Performance[Performance$Activity.type=='B']); qqline(...)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex3a — Effect plot for categorical predictor
nodes.content: Visualize the effect of a categorical predictor on the response using an effects plot. --- **Answer.** `effects::Effect(...)` shows fitted means (and 95% CIs) for each level of the categorical predictor, holding other variables at their typical values. Useful for interpreting models with interactions/categorical predictors. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `library(effects)` `mod <- lm(response ~ Medallion + ..., data=Performance)` `plot(Effect('Medallion', mod))` %%/RBLOCK%%
